(B) 2400 m equates 1500 m with the INITIAL remaining fraction 5/8 (1500 = 5T/8), the same confusion at the start of the shift. (A) 2000 m equates 1500 m with the total DONE fraction after the shift, 3/4 (1500 = 3T/4), forgetting that some pipe was already laid before the shift. (E) 12000 m comes from mis-computing the fractional drop as 1/8 instead of 3/8 (e.g., mis-subtracting 5/8 − 1/4) and solving 1500 = T/8. Only the complementary-fraction difference 3/8 correctly maps the measured 1500 m to the whole.

stem: The diagram shows part of the graph of a function y = |ax + b| (with a and b real constants). Point P lies on the left-hand branch. Two other points on the graph are joined by a dashed horizontal segment because they sit at the same height. Reading only the values shown on the graph, find the x-coordinate of the point on the right-hand branch that lies at the same height as P.
explanation: A V-shaped graph y = |ax + b| is symmetric about the vertical line through its vertex, so two points have equal height exactly when they are equidistant from the vertex abscissa. The figure gives no formula, so the vertex must be located from the two equal-height points, which sit at x = 0 and x = 7; the axis of symmetry is their midpoint, x = (0 + 7)/2 = 3.5. Point P is at x = −2, and its mirror image across x = 3.5 is x = 2(3.5) − (−2) = 9 (correct, A). Distractor B (16) uses the marked point x = 7 as the axis of symmetry instead of the true vertex: 2(7) − (−2) = 16. Distractor C (5) drops the sign of P and reflects x = +2 about 3.5: 2(3.5) − 2 = 5. Distractor D (2) assumes symmetry about the y-axis, giving −(−2) = 2. Distractor E (5.5) adds P's distance-from-origin |−2| = 2 to the vertex (3.5 + 2) instead of P's true distance 5.5 from the vertex. Only x = 9 is equidistant from x = 3.5 as P.

stem:
In a negative-feedback amplifier the measured closed-loop gain G is related to the internal open-loop gain A and a fixed feedback fraction β by the relation

  G = A / (1 + βA).

An engineer knows G and β and wants to recover the open-loop gain A. Solving the relation for A gives A =
explanation:
Cross-multiply: G(1 + βA) = A, so G + βGA = A. The target variable A now appears on BOTH sides — that collection step is what makes the item selective. Gather A: G = A − βGA = A(1 − βG), hence A = G/(1 − βG). Option A is correct.

Distractor traps:
B) G/(1 + βG): keeps the +βGA on the wrong side, writing G = A(1 + βG) — a sign slip in collecting the shared A term (the classic error absent from a one-sided invert).
C) G/(βG − 1): factors as A(βG − 1) = G, negating the whole denominator (sign reversal of the isolated group).
D) G(1 − βG): correctly finds the factor (1 − βG) but multiplies instead of dividing by it — failure to isolate.
E) (1 − βG)/G: inverts the final fraction (reciprocal error), a rote symmetry guess.
Each distractor is a distinct, plausible rational form; none is also correct and none is trivially eliminable.

stem:
In a gearbox, three shafts rotate at steady angular speeds a, b and c (in rad/s). The mechanical couplings between the shafts impose the two exact relations

  3a = 8b   and   6b = 5c.

Express c in terms of a.
explanation:
The middle variable b must be eliminated. From 3a = 8b, correctly rearranged, b = (3/8)a. From 6b = 5c, correctly rearranged, c = (6/5)b. Substituting: c = (6/5)(3/8)a = 18/40 a = (9/20)a. So A is correct.

Each distractor is a distinct rearrangement error:
- B (3/5)a: the student assumes b simply "cancels," treating the two equations as 3a = 5c (dropping the 8 and 6 coefficients that belong to b), giving c = (3/5)a.
- C (5/16)a: the second relation is inverted — writing c = (5/6)b instead of c = (6/5)b — so (5/6)(3/8) = 5/16.
- D (16/5)a: the first relation is inverted — writing b = (8/3)a instead of (3/8)a — so (6/5)(8/3) = 16/5.
- E (20/9)a: both relations are inverted (b = (8/3)a and c = (5/6)b), compounding both mistakes into (5/6)(8/3) = 20/9.

Only A applies the ratio of coefficients correctly to both stages. The distractors have magnitudes both below and above 1, so none can be eliminated by a quick sanity check — the item is decided purely by correct rearrangement and elimination.

stem: A block is given an initial speed of 8.0 m/s straight UP a rough incline at 30° to the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is μ = 0.30 and cos30° ≈ 0.87. The block travels up, momentarily stops, and (because tan30° > μ) slides back down. Using g = 9.8 m/s², what is its speed when it returns to the launch point?
choices: 0 m/s (the block stays at rest at the top)
explanation: Going up, deceleration = g(sinθ + μcosθ) = 9.8(0.5 + 0.30·0.87) = 7.45 m/s², so distance d = v₀²/(2a_up) = 64/14.9 = 4.30 m. Since tan30° = 0.58 > 0.30 the block slides back with a_down = g(sinθ − μcosθ) = 9.8(0.5 − 0.30·0.87) = 2.35 m/s². Return speed v = √(2·a_down·d) = √(2·2.35·4.30) ≈ 4.5 m/s (B). A = 8.0 assumes energy conservation with no friction. C = 6.5 keeps friction on the way up but takes a frictionless descent. D = 4.3 is the distance travelled up the slope, mistaken for a speed. E = 0 wrongly concludes the block sticks.

stem: A ball is thrown from ground level and must just pass over the top corner of a wall that is 15 m tall and stands 20 m away horizontally (the corner is at coordinates x = 20 m, y = 15 m from the launch point). The launch angle may be chosen freely. Neglecting air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², what is the MINIMUM launch speed for which the ball can reach that corner?
explanation: The minimum speed to pass through a point (x, y) is v_min = √[g(y + √(x²+y²))]. Here √(20²+15²) = 25, so v_min = √[10(15 + 25)] = √400 = 20 m/s (A). B = 28.3 wrongly assumes 45° is optimal (then y = x − gx²/v² forces v² = 800). C = 14.1 uses only the maximum-range condition v² = gx, ignoring the wall's height. D = 17.3 treats it as launching straight up to height 15 m (√(2gy)). E = 15.8 uses √(g·√(x²+y²)), forgetting the extra +y term inside the bracket.

stem: V and W are opposite vertices of a cube and O is its centre, so VW is a space (body) diagonal. A single flat cut is made through O, perpendicular to VW. What is the exact shape of the resulting cross-section?
explanation: A plane through the centre perpendicular to a body diagonal meets all six faces of the cube, cutting each at the midpoint of an edge. The six intersection points are all edge-midpoints and, by the cube's three-fold rotational symmetry about VW, are equally spaced, so the section is a regular hexagon. A square comes only from a cut parallel to a face; an equilateral triangle from slicing off a single corner near V; a non-square rectangle from a cut through two parallel edges; and a regular pentagon is impossible for any planar section of a cube.

stem: La figura mostra lo sviluppo (net) "a scala" (zig-zag) di un cubo, con le sei facce numerate da 1 a 6. Sulle facce 1 e 3 è disegnata una freccia: nel piano del disegno entrambe puntano verso l'alto. Ripiegando lo sviluppo per formare il cubo, quale faccia risulta opposta alla faccia 1 e come risultano orientate, l'una rispetto all'altra, le due frecce disegnate sulle facce 1 e 3?
choices: Faccia opposta alla 1: la faccia 2; le due frecce puntano nella stessa direzione e nello stesso verso (parallele e concordi).
Faccia opposta alla 1: la faccia 2; le due frecce risultano perpendicolari tra loro.
Faccia opposta alla 1: la faccia 4; le due frecce risultano perpendicolari tra loro.
Faccia opposta alla 1: la faccia 4; le due frecce puntano nella stessa direzione ma in versi opposti (parallele e discordi).
Faccia opposta alla 1: la faccia 5; le due frecce puntano nella stessa direzione e nello stesso verso (parallele e concordi).
explanation: Lo sviluppo è "a scala": partendo dalla faccia 1 la striscia prosegue 1–3 (in fila), poi scende 3–5, prosegue 5–2, scende 2–6, prosegue 6–4. Ripiegando questa striscia le coppie di facce opposte risultano 1–2, 3–6, 5–4. Quindi la faccia opposta alla 1 è la 2. Per l'orientamento: le facce 1 e 3 sono adiacenti e, una volta piegate, si incontrano lungo lo spigolo verticale che nel disegno le separa. Entrambe le frecce sono disegnate PARALLELE a quello spigolo di piegatura (puntano verso l'alto). Una freccia parallela alla cerniera di piegatura non viene ruotata dalla piega: resta invariata. Perciò dopo la piega le due frecce restano parallele e concordi. Risposta A. Trappole: B nasconde l'errore più comune, cioè credere che, essendo 1 e 3 su piani perpendicolari, le loro frecce debbano per forza risultare perpendicolari (ignora che le frecce sono parallele allo spigolo di piega). C è la risposta del candidato "addestrato" che applica meccanicamente la regola "opposta = tre passi avanti nella numerazione" (1→4) valida solo per la croce/striscia diritta, e aggiunge la perpendicolarità ingenua. D usa la stessa regola meccanica errata (opposta 4) e in più suppone che la piega inverta il verso della freccia. E ragiona correttamente sulle frecce ma sbaglia la piega, scambiando per opposta una faccia in realtà adiacente alla 1 (la 5).

stem: A 2.0 kg block is released from rest and slides 5.0 m down a first incline angled at 37° above the horizontal (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8), where the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. At the base it crosses a 2.0 m stretch of horizontal floor whose coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.40, and then begins to slide up a second incline, also angled at 37°, whose coefficients of friction are μ_k = 0.25 and μ_s = 0.80. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting the size of the block and any energy loss at the two corners, what does the block do?
choices: It stops 1.5 m up the second incline and stays there.
It stops 1.5 m up the second incline, then slides back down.
It stops 2.0 m up the second incline and stays there.
It stops 2.5 m up the second incline and stays there.
It never reaches the second incline; it comes to rest on the floor.
explanation: Energy bookkeeping to the foot of the second incline: on incline 1 the net driving force is mg(sinθ − μ_k cosθ) = 20(0.6 − 0.25·0.8) = 8 N, so KE at the base = 8·5.0 = 40 J. Crossing the floor loses μ·mg·L = 0.40·20·2.0 = 16 J, leaving 24 J entering incline 2. Going up, BOTH gravity and friction decelerate the block: force = mg(sinθ + μ_k cosθ) = 20(0.6 + 0.2) = 16 N, so it climbs d = 24/16 = 1.5 m. The decisive step is what happens once it is momentarily at rest: the down-slope gravity component is mg sinθ = 12 N, while the maximum static friction is μ_s·mg cosθ = 0.80·(20·0.8) = 12.8 N. Since 12.8 N > 12 N (equivalently μ_s = 0.80 > tanθ = 0.75), static friction holds it — it stays. Hence A. B has the correct 1.5 m but fails the static check, wrongly assuming a block on a 37° incline must slide back (it would only slide if μ_s < tanθ, e.g. using μ_k = 0.25 by mistake). C = 2.0 m omits kinetic friction during the ascent (uses 24/12, gravity only). D = 2.5 m forgets the floor's 16 J loss (uses 40/16). E assumes the block never makes it across the floor by overcounting floor friction; in fact 24 J of KE remains, so it does start up the incline.

stem:
Without using a calculator, arrange the following five real numbers in increasing order:

  3/2,  π/2,  5/π,  8/5,  π²/6.

(Recall only that π ≈ 3.14; all five values lie very close together, so each pair must be compared exactly by cross-multiplication rather than by rounding.)
explanation:
Because 3/2 = 1.5, π/2 ≈ 1.571, 5/π ≈ 1.592, 8/5 = 1.600 and π²/6 ≈ 1.645 all sit within a span of 0.15, rounding π to 3.14 is not enough; each adjacent pair reduces to comparing a power of π with a nearby round number, and the tension is that these "just barely" comparisons point in OPPOSITE directions. Cross-multiply each adjacent pair (all quantities positive):

• 3/2 vs π/2  ⟺  3 vs π  →  π > 3, so 3/2 < π/2 (3/2 is the smallest).
• π/2 vs 5/π  ⟺  π² vs 10  →  π² ≈ 9.87 < 10, so π/2 < 5/π.
• 5/π vs 8/5  ⟺  25 vs 8π  →  8π ≈ 25.13 > 25, so 5/π < 8/5.
• 8/5 vs π²/6 ⟺  48 vs 5π²  →  5π² ≈ 49.35 > 48, so 8/5 < π²/6.

Hence 3/2 < π/2 < 5/π < 8/5 < π²/6, which is B. The correct answer is exactly the ordering produced by the true value of π, whose two binding facts are π² < 10 (upper bound π < 3.162) and 8π > 25 (lower bound π > 3.125): the candidate must effectively pin π into the narrow band (3.125, 3.162).

Each distractor is the ordering obtained from a specific WRONG estimate of π:
• A — overestimating π so that π² > 10 (π ≳ 3.16). This flips only the π/2 vs 5/π comparison, moving 5/π below π/2. It is the classic error of rounding π² up to 10 instead of using π² ≈ 9.87.
• C — using π slightly too small so that 8π < 25 (π < 3.125). This flips only the ultra-tight 5/π vs 8/5 pair, so 8/5 is wrongly placed before 5/π. It comes from rounding 8π down to 25.
• D — using π ≈ 3.10, which makes π³ < 30 (π³ ≈ 31 is the true fact). Believing π³ < 30 forces 5/π above π²/6, so 5/π is wrongly ranked as the largest of all five.
• E — a gross underestimate π ≈ 3.05 giving π² < 9.6, which pushes π²/6 down below both 8/5 and 5/π and again puts 5/π on top; it is the "π is barely above 3" misconception.

All five options agree that 3/2 is smallest (since π > 3 is universally known), so no option is eliminable by inspection; discriminating them requires resolving the two "just barely" facts π² < 10 and 8π > 25 in opposite directions, which is the intended reasoning.
